The clinical picture strongly favors drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (DI-AIN). Key diagnostic anchors are: (1) classic triad — fever, flank pain, and AKI — occurring after exposure to high-risk medications (cephalexin and omeprazole, both well-documented causes of DI-AIN); (2) sterile pyuria with leukocyturia; (3) urinary cytospin showing 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm — a highly specific finding for renal eosinophilic infiltration, consistent with interstitial eosinophil recruitment in AIN; (4) absence of alternative explanations — no dysuria/frequency (argues against cystitis/pyelonephritis), no hematuria or systemic inflammatory features (reduces likelihood of vasculitis or autoimmune glomerulonephritis), and no evidence of obstruction or structural disease (though ultrasound is pending, the clinical context makes obstruction unlikely). Discontinuation of both agents is appropriate and aligns with standard management.

- Elevated serum creatinine confirming acute kidney injury  
- Sterile leukocyturia (leukocyturia with negative bacterial culture)  
- Urinary cytospin shows 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm — pathognomonic for renal eosinophilic infiltration in AIN

- Absence of urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency, hematuria) — argues against lower UTI or glomerulonephritis  
- Absence of systemic inflammatory signs (chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash) — reduces likelihood of vasculitis or systemic infection

- Absolute eosinophil count (AEC) — would help support (but not rule in/out) AIN; normal AEC does not exclude DI-AIN  
- ANCA panel (MPO/PR3) — needed to definitively exclude pauci-immune vasculitis, especially given AKI and sterile pyuria  
- Renal ultrasound — required to exclude obstructive uropathy or structural renal disease as alternative cause of AKI  
- CBC differential — to assess for peripheral eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes  
- Serum IgE — though low yield, may support hypersensitivity mechanism if elevated  
- Baseline vs. current eGFR/creatinine values — to characterize severity and trajectory of AKI  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical picture strongly favors drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (DI-AIN). Key diagnostic anchors are: (1) classic triad — fever, flank pain, and AKI — occurring after exposure to high-risk medications (cephalexin and omeprazole, both well-documented causes of DI-AIN); (2) sterile pyuria with leukocyturia; (3) urinary cytospin showing 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm — a highly specific finding for renal eosinophilic infiltration, consistent with interstitial eosinophil recruitment in AIN; (4) absence of alternative explanations — no dysuria/frequency (argues against cystitis/pyelonephritis), no hematuria or systemic inflammatory features (reduces likelihood of vasculitis or autoimmune glomerulonephritis), and no evidence of obstruction or structural disease (though ultrasound is pending, the clinical context makes obstruction unlikely). While eosinophilia on peripheral smear or elevated serum IgE would further support AIN, their absence does not exclude it — up to 30–50% of DI-AIN cases lack peripheral eosinophilia. The cytologic finding of eosinophilic cells in urine is more specific than peripheral AEC for renal-limited eosinophilic inflammation. Pauci-immune vasculitis (e.g., MPO-ANCA vasculitis) remains a critical alternative, but it typically presents with active urinary sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts), systemic symptoms (weight loss, rash, pulmonary involvement), and often more severe AKI — none of which are present here. The absence of hematuria, night sweats, or weight loss makes vasculitis less likely. Omeprazole is a particularly common cause of chronic or subacute AIN, and cephalexin is a classic beta-lactam trigger — the combination increases suspicion. Discontinuation of both agents is appropriate and aligns with standard management.

- Fever, non-localized flank pain, and persistent fatigue following resolution of sinusitis — consistent with systemic inflammatory response in AIN

- Urinary cytospin shows 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm — pathognomonic for renal eosinophilic infiltration in AIN  
- Temporal association with recent cephalexin and chronic omeprazole use — both established causes of DI-AIN

- Absence of systemic inflammatory signs (chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash) — reduces likelihood of vasculitis or systemic infection  

[GAPS]  
- Absolute eosinophil count (AEC) — would help support (but not rule in/out) AIN; normal AEC does not exclude DI-AIN  
- ANCA panel (MPO/PR3) — needed to definitively exclude pauci-immune vasculitis, especially given AKI and sterile pyuria  
- Renal ultrasound — required to exclude obstructive uropathy or structural renal disease as alternative cause of AKI  
- CBC differential — to assess for peripheral eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes  
- Serum IgE — though low yield, may support hypersensitivity mechanism if elevated  
- Baseline vs. current eGFR/creatinine values — to characterize severity and trajectory of AKI  

[DIAGNOSIS]
